passages.quote:
If persistent angular changes arrive repeatedly, their errors accumulate. Divide time into intervals of length $\Delta t$. Let $\xi_j$ be the change in the represented coordinate during interval $j$. The calculation assumes:

- increments are independent;
- each increment has mean zero;
- each increment has variance $2D\Delta t$, where $D$ has units coordinate squared per time.

After $n$ intervals,

$$
\theta_n-\theta_0=\sum_{j=1}^{n}\xi_j,
\qquad
\operatorname{Var}(\theta_n-\theta_0)
=\sum_{j=1}^{n}\operatorname{Var}(\xi_j)
=2Dn\Delta t.
$$

Writing $t=n\Delta t$ gives linear variance growth $2Dt$. To describe this limit with a continuous path, use [**Brownian motion**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} $W(t)$. It starts at zero, has continuous paths and independent Gaussian increments with mean zero, and satisfies $\operatorname{Var}[W(t)-W(s)]=t-s$ for $t\geq s$. It describes the limit of many small, suitably independent fluctuations. A physical network need only approach this description over the time and noise scales relevant to the calculation.

In this continuous diffusion approximation,

$$
\theta(t)=\theta(0)+\sqrt{2D}\,W(t),
\qquad
\mathbb E[(\theta(t)-\theta(0))^2]=2Dt.
$$

The parameter $D$ is the diffusion coefficient. It measures the rate of variance growth; a single trajectory need not move monotonically away from its starting value.

The mean squared displacement, or MSD, is the expected squared change across a lag. In the zero-mean diffusion just defined, MSD is $2Dt$. A [**root mean squared displacement**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} is its square root, $\sqrt{2Dt}$, and has the same units as the represented coordinate. In several dimensions, adding independent coordinate contributions gives an overall MSD of $2dDt$ only when each of the $d$ coordinates has the same diffusion coefficient. A paper that defines its diffusion parameter as the entire two-dimensional MSD slope uses a different convention.

Take an illustrative angular diffusion coefficient $D=0.02$ degrees squared per second. At 0.35 s its variance is $0.014$ degrees squared and its root mean squared displacement is 0.118 degrees, or about 7.10 arcminutes. At 1 s the root mean squared displacement is 0.20 degrees. These are teaching values, not a new estimate from either monkey. If there is also a constant bias velocity $v=0.10$ degrees per second, then $$ \theta(t)-\theta(0)=vt+\sqrt{2D}\,W(t), \qquad \operatorname{MSD}(t)=v^2t^2+2Dt. $$ The deterministic and random contributions are equal at $t=2D/v^2=4$ seconds. Their equal contributions there are each $0.16$ degrees squared. At longer times the bias dominates this unbounded model even though it was small over a short observation. A theory of random diffusion must therefore account for systematic drift separately. Sample paths show the irregular motion; exact displacement scales show how its spread differs from a fixed bias.
{{block:fig:FOUNDATIONS-DIFFUSION-BIAS}}
A single path can turn back toward zero even while the root mean squared displacement grows. A constant bias grows linearly, so it eventually exceeds the square root growth of the random displacement scale. See [Gaussian displacement density, SI Eq. S30, p. 7](../papers/burak-fiete-2012-persistent-activity-si.pdf#page=7). Two times along a Brownian path are correlated even though its increments are independent. For $0\leq s\leq t$, write $W(t)=W(s)+[W(t)-W(s)]$. The bracketed increment is independent of $W(s)$ and has mean zero, giving $$ \operatorname{Cov}(W(s),W(t)) =\operatorname{Var}(W(s))=s, \qquad \operatorname{Cov}(W(s),W(t))=\min(s,t). $$ The same argument gives covariance $2D\min(s,t)$ for a diffusing coordinate started at a fixed value. This identity is the intermediate step needed to compute the error from averaging a memory that moves during readout. It also helps explain why smoothing a diffusive input is different from smoothing a stationary noise source. A finite range, a periodic coordinate, external feedback, or a position-dependent diffusion coefficient changes long-time behavior. For example, ordinary squared angular distance on a ring cannot keep growing linearly forever. The basic $2Dt$ result is local or unbounded unless those conditions are treated separately.

- [**Brownian motion:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} A continuous random process starting at zero with independent Gaussian increments of mean zero and variance equal to elapsed time.

changes_reviewed.reason: The process is now defined before its displacement equation. Starting at zero, continuous paths, independent Gaussian increments of mean zero and variance equal to lag specify standard Brownian motion. Multiplication by sqrt(2D) then gives mean-zero displacement variance2Dt, and the subsequent bias comparison and shared-increment covariance remain correct. The many-small-fluctuations claim retains its suitable-independence and physical-approximation limits. No new required concept is introduced.

passages.quote:
For $m$ memory coordinates the information is a matrix,

$$
J_{\alpha\beta}=\sum_i
\frac{\partial_{\theta_\alpha}\bar r_i\,
\partial_{\theta_\beta}\bar r_i}{\bar r_i}.
$$

The matrix bound $2D\succeq\tau^{-2}J^{-1}$ means that every linear combination of coordinate displacements obeys the corresponding variance lower bound. Here $A\succeq B$ means $\mathbf z^T(A-B)\mathbf z\ge0$ for every real vector $\mathbf z$. To derive it, form $N\times m$ matrices $U_{i\alpha}=u_i^\alpha/\sqrt{\bar r_i}$ and $V_{i\alpha}=v_i^\alpha\sqrt{\bar r_i}$. Then

$$
U^TV=I,\qquad U^TU=\tau^2J,\qquad V^TV=2D.
$$

The matrix inequality applies when every independent small coordinate change can be distinguished through a change in rates, so $J$ is invertible. It also explains why a scalar bound in each coordinate separately would miss coupled directions.[^p1-matrix]

::: {.publisher-clarification-note .publisher-fold-always title="Check: the residual matrix proves the lower bound"}

Set $Q=V-U(U^TU)^{-1}$. Expanding $Q^TQ$ and using $U^TV=I$ gives

$$
Q^TQ=V^TV-(U^TU)^{-1}
=2D-\tau^{-2}J^{-1}\succeq0.

The paper also links tuning width to memory persistence. The reason for its opposite predictions in one and three dimensions can be derived from the number of active cells and their slopes. This derivation is a teaching reconstruction of the tuning width argument cited in the main text, rather than a proof that every tuning family follows one power law.[^p1-width]

Assume preferred positions $\mathbf c$ have uniform density $\rho$ in a $d$ dimensional stimulus or memory space. Away from boundaries, let identical tuning curves have fixed peak rate $a$ and a common shape $f$:

$$
\bar r_{\mathbf c}(\boldsymbol\theta)
=a f[(\boldsymbol\theta-\mathbf c)/w].
$$

The width $w$ is varied while $a$, $\rho$, and the shape $f$ are fixed. For one coordinate direction $\alpha$, replace the population sum by an integral and substitute $\mathbf z=(\boldsymbol\theta-\mathbf c)/w$:

$$
J_{\alpha\alpha}
\simeq\rho\int d^d c\,
\frac{a^2w^{-2}(\partial_\alpha f)^2}{af}
=\rho a w^{d-2}
\int d^d z\,\frac{(\partial_\alpha f)^2}{f}.
$$

Two factors determine how information changes with tuning width:

- The volume element contributes $w^d$ because broader fields recruit more neurons.
- The squared slope contributes $w^{-2}$ because broader curves change more slowly.

Each diagonal entry therefore scales as $J_{\alpha\alpha}\propto w^{d-2}$. Now restrict the tuning shape $f$ to depend only on distance from its center. Uniformly distributing those centers makes every coordinate direction equivalent: off-diagonal information terms vanish, and all diagonal entries are equal. For an exponential network that attains the matrix bound, $D_{\alpha\alpha}=1/(2\tau^2J_{\alpha\alpha})\propto w^{2-d}$. The resulting comparisons are:

- Narrower curves help in $d=1$.
- Width has no leading effect in $d=2$.
- Broader curves help in $d=3$.

These conclusions change under another resource constraint. Fixing the total population spike rate instead of peak rate makes $a\propto w^{-d}$, giving $J\propto w^{-2}$ in every dimension. Sparse coverage, a large baseline rate, finite boundaries, correlated noise, or a width too small for the population integral can also change the comparison. Attaining equality means the network reaches the diffusion lower bound for its information rate and synaptic time constant. Minimizing diffusion still requires deciding how much information the allowed architecture and firing budget can supply.

If an external stimulus produces the same tuning curves as the network's input free memory states, the sensory and internal Fisher information are equal. In a symmetric exponential network, maximizing this information then improves sensory estimation and minimizes memory diffusion together. This is why the paper suggests that one circuit could support both sensory estimation and memory storage. The mathematical compatibility does not establish where a particular animal stores a memory, and the equality of tuning curves must be checked rather than inferred from the shared formula.[^p1-colocation]

changes_reviewed.reason: The reader has the information matrix, its inverse bound and the scalar-coordinate integral before the new restriction. Radial tuning shape with uniform centers makes diagonal entries equal and cross-direction integrands cancel by reflection, within the stated continuum/away-from-boundaries comparison. Equality in the matrix bound then gives D_aa=(2tau squared J_aa)^-1 and the correct w^(2-d) law. The new text explains the directional condition without relying on the later word isotropy. It keeps resource, equality and boundary limits. No new unprovided specialist dependency.

part1_purpose.text: A stable population pattern can retain a continuous value while fluctuations move that value along its family of persistent states. These chapters establish the neural and probability background, derive the surviving motion, and connect it to limits on information and readout.
part1_purpose.reason: It gives the common question, stable activity with wandering represented value, then the neural/probability setup, surviving motion and information/readout limits in their actual chapter order. Reading-guide memory overview supplies a plain preview; no calculation relies on the Part purpose to teach an unfamiliar technical definition.

global_description.text: This guide teaches the neural background and central derivations of Burak and Fiete (2012), Ben-Shushan and colleagues (2022), and Mainali and colleagues (2025). Begin with the reading path for paper copies, assumed knowledge, and the route through the mathematics.
global_description.verdict: accurate and adequate for metadata/landing description
global_description.reason: It identifies the three-paper scope and directs the reader to the reading path for baseline knowledge, sources and mathematics; the full introduction supplies the actual teaching frame.

caption_alt_width.caption: Memory loss and eye drift concern changes over time; place-field statistics concern variation across a fixed spatial map. The eye pathway shows the proposed changing-command mechanism. Original guide schematic based on the three papers, with illustrative traces rather than recorded data.
caption_alt_width.alt: Three separate rows compare a wandering stored value over time, a proposed changing command passing through muscles to eye position, and one fixed spatial rate curve evaluated twice at the same place. They link to the 2012 memory, 2022 eye-drift and 2025 place-field papers respectively.

map_review.conclusion: Approved for the existing map label repair only. No new illustration content or size change.

overall_conclusion: All three focused Stage1 repairs pass correctness, adequacy and dependency recheck. No open Stage1 memory finding remains on this proposed snapshot. This does not claim Stage2,Stage3 or final rendered-book acceptance.
